clue.text: Faltering train too slow at English end of Channel rail link

indicators.note: something faltering stumbles and loses its order, so the letters that follow get rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A sluggish train limps into the British terminus of the Channel Tunnel service.
explanation.walkthrough: When this puzzle appeared, Eurostar trains from Paris and Brussels ran into London's Waterloo, so the London terminal is literally the English end of the link.
explanation.definitionFit: The London terminus served Eurostar trains through the Channel Tunnel until 2007, making it the line's British terminal.

clue.text: In practice, comprehensive type of characters

annotation.answer: THE QUICK BROWN FOX JUMPS OVER THE LAZY DOG

definitions.text: In practice, comprehensive type of characters

blocks.clueFragment: In practice, comprehensive type of characters
blocks.note: surface reading: a thorough sort of people, as they behave in real life
setter's reading: a sentence used for typing practice that includes every letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone sizing up a group of people as all-round types when actually put to the test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' and 'characters' look like personality words, but they mean typing and letters: the sentence is the classic pangram typists use for practice.
explanation.definitionFit: This famous sentence contains all twenty-six letters, so typists and font designers use it for testing keyboards and displaying typefaces.

clue.text: TV and newspapers offering "Ken Dodd's No Con"

indicators.note: no here means without, so the letters of the word after it are taken away

blocks.note: Ken Dodd was a famous Liverpool stand-up, an example of the profession
taken as written; its letters are scattered at both ends of the profession word

explanation.surface: Broadcasters and papers splash a story clearing the entertainer Ken Dodd of trickery.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove C, O and N from COMEDIAN and MEDIA is left. The surface recalls Dodd's 1989 acquittal on tax charges, widely covered by the press.
explanation.definitionFit: Television, radio and the press together are collectively called the mass communication industry, the plural of medium.

clue.text: Stop for a few minutes jazz by Brubeck

blocks.note: first meaning: have a short break
second meaning: the famous 1959 Dave Brubeck Quartet tune in 5/4 time

explanation.surface: A jazz fan pauses a Brubeck record for a short interval.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means pause briefly for a rest, and it is also the title of Paul Desmond's tune recorded by the Brubeck Quartet.

clue.text: My word shows where initially to place C for Constraint

blocks.clueFragment: shows where initially to place C for Constraint
blocks.note: surface reading: an instruction about spelling out an abbreviation

blocks.clueFragment: where initially to place C for Constraint
blocks.note: setter's reading: a word for constraint is spelt by putting C at the front, next to a mild oath

explanation.surface: A puzzled exclamation at a fiddly rule about where the letter C belongs.
explanation.walkthrough: CHECK means constraint; to make it you put C initially, beside HECK. So the answer both names where C goes and is an exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: This northern English expression of surprise works like other mild exclamations such as goodness or blimey.

clue.text: See 2
Run out of gear

blocks.note: surface reading: a car or bike running in neutral, or a runner short of kit
setter's reading: gear is clothing, so this is running without any clothes on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gear' suggests a gearbox, but here it is clothing: a run naked, as at a sports ground, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To dash naked through a public place, typically a sports event, is the slang verb here.

clue.text: Isaac N. hit tree; it shook: what (disastrously) went down must come up?

definitions.text: what (disastrously) went down must come up?

indicators.note: shaking something tumbles its contents about, so the preceding words get jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Isaac Newton bumps a tree, and his gravity rule is turned upside down for a famous sunken liner.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reverses Newton's 'what goes up must come down'. The answer is the title of a 1976 novel and 1980 film about salvaging the liner.
explanation.definitionFit: Bringing the wrecked liner back to the surface would mean the ship that sank in 1912 must be lifted.

clue.text: He plays piano and conducts because "Misty" inspires knowledge

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one word takes another inside it

blocks.note: as can mean because
synonym
ken is knowledge, as in beyond my ken

explanation.surface: A musician's career is explained by a dreamy song giving him insight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misty' looks like the jazz standard, but it is just a synonym for hazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Vladimir Ashkenazy is a celebrated Russian-born concert pianist who has also worked as a symphony conductor.

clue.text: Extremist in the sinful tradition

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the following words

blocks.note: the end of sinful and the start of tradition

explanation.surface: A zealot clinging to a wicked custom.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultra is a person holding extreme views, especially in politics or as a football fan.

clue.text: Ask Pole to change title on letter

indicators.note: one magnetic pole is swapped for the other, north becoming south

blocks.note: synonym
S, south, replaces N, north, the other pole

explanation.surface: Someone asks a Polish man to change the form of address on a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person; it is the north and south pole letters N and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Esq. is the courtesy title written after a man's name when addressing an envelope, mainly in British usage.

clue.text: Daily newspaper's gone out of business?

blocks.clueFragment: Daily newspaper's gone out of business?
blocks.note: surface reading: a paper has closed down
setter's reading: a former press, a printing press that is no more

explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Express is a British national paper; split the name as ex-press and it is a press that has gone out of business.
explanation.definitionFit: The Daily Express is a long-running British national tabloid published every morning.

clue.text: Den sounds like hen

indicators.note: says to go by how a word is spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: a hen is a layer of eggs

explanation.surface: A plain statement comparing a den with a hen.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild animal's hidden resting place, and by extension a person's private hideaway, is a synonym.

clue.text: Fagin's boy, Dickens' Herbert, gets on Dickens' wick

blocks.note: the part that goes on wick to make Pickwick, Dickens' novel
Herbert Pocket is Pip's friend in Great Expectations

explanation.surface: One of Fagin's lads irritates a Dickens character, since 'gets on one's wick' is British slang for annoys.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'gets on Dickens' wick' as what sits on 'wick' in Dickens' The Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Fagin in Oliver Twist runs a gang of boys trained to steal from people's coats, like the Artful Dodger.

clue.text: 500 sheets amongst 550 - and that's heaven in bed

indicators.note: something placed amongst others is surrounded by them

blocks.note: Roman numerals: D is 500 and L is 50
a ream is a pack of 500 sheets of paper
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sheets counted in hundreds, then blissful bedtime, as if a laundry tally ended in sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: The imaginary realm of sleep and dreams is the blissful place you drift into once asleep.

clue.text: Common sight in the park: toe broken with rake

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces that can be put back in any order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener in a park hurts a foot on a rake.
explanation.definitionFit: A large native deciduous species found growing in many British parks and woods.

clue.text: Shake a lot during large drink

indicators.note: during means within, so one piece falls inside the other

blocks.note: a treble is a triple measure of spirits
M is a thousand in Roman numerals, a lot

explanation.surface: Someone quivers violently in the middle of a big drinking session.
explanation.definitionFit: To quake or quiver, as with fear or cold, means much the same as the verb in the clue.

clue.text: South goes west and Motorway sign's the same

indicators.note: in a down clue west is left, so the letter is placed in front

blocks.note: a thou is slang for the number the M sign stands for, so it is the same
abbreviation
taken as written

explanation.surface: Driving directions: head south, then west, and the motorway signs agree.
explanation.walkthrough: British motorways are marked M, which is also the Roman numeral for a thousand; 'the same' points back to that number.
explanation.definitionFit: M labels British motorways, and as a Roman numeral that letter stands for one thousand.

clue.text: See 2
See 2
Bad feeling of mine aggravated gutless Tony

indicators.note: without guts means the inside is removed and only the ends remain
aggravated means stirred up and disturbed, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written
first and last letters of Tony

explanation.surface: Someone's resentment is stirred up against a cowardly man called Tony.
explanation.definitionFit: Hostility or mutual hatred between people is a feeling of ill will.

clue.text: Shakespearean character this year in city

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: the English cathedral city
the puzzle appeared in 1999, and 99 can be written IC in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare figure is appearing in a city's theatre this year.
explanation.walkthrough: IC for 99 is an informal Roman form (strictly XCIX), standing for 1999, the year the puzzle was published.
explanation.definitionFit: The dead jester whose skull Hamlet holds while saying 'Alas, poor ...' is a famous figure from the play.

clue.text: Desert means to leave twice?

blocks.note: synonym
the prefix meaning twice, as in biannual

explanation.surface: A riddle: does deserting mean leaving two times?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' looks like a verb meaning leave; it is the noun, the arid region.
explanation.definitionFit: The vast arid region spanning Mongolia and northern China is a well-known example of the noun.

clue.text: Colour of mint with a hole, of course

blocks.note: first meaning: the shade of the herb's leaves
second meaning: the closely mown area round each hole on a golf course

explanation.surface: Describing a mint sweet with a hole in the middle, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: Mint with a hole suggests the Polo, a ring-shaped mint sweet, but 'of course' is a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the herb's leaf colour and the putting surface around each flag on a golf course share this name.

clue.text: Glass flipper

blocks.note: first meaning: a flat-bottomed drinking vessel
second meaning: an acrobat who does somersaults and flips

explanation.walkthrough: 'Glass flipper' sounds like a seal's or a diver's fin; the words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A straight-sided drinking vessel and a gymnast performing somersaults share the same name.

clue.text: Gray's Inn almost turned lilac

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
turned means rearranged into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, the London legal society

explanation.surface: One of London's Inns of Court, where barristers train, has nearly gone purple.
explanation.definitionFit: The botanical genus name covers the lilacs, and is also used loosely for mock orange.

clue.text: Frequently decimal?

blocks.note: first meaning: many times
second meaning, split in two words: belonging to the number ten

explanation.walkthrough: Decimal means relating to tens, so it can be read as two short words, 'of ten'; the question mark flags the liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb for something happening many times or regularly is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Down these tubes vessel shot - one nil!

indicators.note: shot can mean ruined or broken, so the letters that follow are disordered

blocks.note: a can is a container
taken as written

explanation.surface: A football commentary: a ship's shot goes down the tubes, and it's one-nil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' is the verb to eat: these are tubes you down. The usual spelling has a double L.
explanation.definitionFit: Cannelloni is Italian pasta shaped like large tubes, stuffed and baked, which you swallow.
